Pearson-Corrected Similarity Between Two Feature Sets

Source: R/metrics.R
pearson_similarity.Rd

Computes a Pearson-correlation-inspired similarity that corrects for expected random intersection. This is a second chance-correction approach (alongside adjusted_similarity()) that normalises by the geometric mean of the within-set variances under independent Bernoulli sampling.

Usage

pearson_similarity(
  set1 = NULL,
  set2 = NULL,
  n_universe = NULL,
  list_i = NULL,
  list_j = NULL,
  d = NULL
)

Arguments

set1

Character or integer vector of selected feature identifiers.

set2

Character or integer vector of selected feature identifiers.

n_universe

Integer; total number of candidate features in the universe.

list_i

Deprecated; use set1 instead. If supplied by name, a deprecation warning is emitted and the value is used as set1 when the latter is NULL. It will be removed in a future release.

list_j

Deprecated; use set2 instead. If supplied by name, a deprecation warning is emitted and the value is used as set2 when the latter is NULL. It will be removed in a future release.

d

Deprecated; use n_universe instead. If supplied by name, a deprecation warning is emitted and the value is used as n_universe when the latter is NULL. It will be removed in a future release.

Value

Numeric scalar. Positive values indicate more overlap than chance; the maximum is exactly 1 for identical non-degenerate sets (the statistic is the phi coefficient).

Details

The formula is: $$S_{\text{Pearson}}(A, B) = \frac{r - k_i k_j / d}{d \cdot \upsilon_i \upsilon_j}$$ where \(r = |A \cap B|\), \(k_i = |A_i|\), \(d\) is the universe size, and \(\upsilon_i = \sqrt{\pi_i (1 - \pi_i)}\) with \(\pi_i = k_i / d\).

Edge cases: returns 1 when both sets are empty or both equal the universe; returns 0 when one set is empty or equals the universe.

See also

pearson_similarity_pairwise() for computing all pairwise values at once, pearson_similarity_summary() for a summary statistic, adjusted_similarity() for an alternative chance-correction.

Examples

pearson_similarity(c("f1","f2","f3"), c("f2","f3","f4"), n_universe = 10L)
#> [1] 0.5238095
pearson_similarity(c("f1","f2"),      c("f1","f2"),      n_universe = 10L) # exactly 1
#> [1] 1
pearson_similarity(character(0),      c("f1","f2"),      n_universe = 10L) # 0
#> [1] 0
